steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on model arithmetic, a method for controlled text generation that combines multiple language models and classifiers through formulas, plus a speculative-sampling extension that makes it efficient. Cover how LLMs are controlled today, what is missing, our method and our contributions.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
(opening)
- LLMs (cite) recognized for handling wide range of tasks (cite)
- chatbots for children, students, customers -> need precise control of vocabulary, linguistic style, emotional expression

## Controlling Language Models
- prompting with natural language (cite): simple, conditions on broad attribute; hard to express how present the attribute should be
- can't reliably steer away; mentioning a topic can raise its likelihood (cite), e.g. "do not mention cats"
- fine-tuning: needs highly specific data, data implicitly encodes strength
- CTG: steer during inference (cite); condition on attribute a smoothly by biasing token distribution
- Bayes rule P(\text{text}|a)\propto P(a|\text{text})P(\text{text}); auxiliary model P(a|\text{text}) conditions the LLM P(\text{text}) towards a

## Key Challenge
- drawbacks: expressiveness, efficiency, interpretability
- strength parameter \lambda ad hoc: exponential weight P(a|\text{text})^{\lambda}; unintuitive, no Bayesian interpretation e.g. biasing away
- neither prompting nor CTG: natural, controlled combination of multiple attributes with relative strength
  - ambiguity of natural language (cite); no theory/semantics for \lambda
- CTG and fine-tuning need custom data (cite), resource-intensive (cite), multiple models at inference

## Model Arithmetic
- principled, intuitive way to combine multiple models
- orthogonal to prompting, fine-tuning, simple CTG (classifiers); incorporates them
- blend LLMs and attributes into one formula-based composite model
- Fig. 1: magical, child-like fairy tale; models M_{a} with attributes a
  - prompted \bm{{M_{\text{child}}}}: child-appropriate but not child-like
  - subtract \bm{{M_{\text{adult}}}} with weight 0.6
  - bias with classifier \bm{{C_{\text{formal}}}} to increase formality again
  - \unionop operator: magical + child-like, further bias
- not precisely expressible with prior CTG; flexible, precise control of each component
- prompting / fine-tuning for individual M and C; many prior CTG techniques as formulas (Section 3)

## Speculative Sampling
- CTG incl. model arithmetic -> more inference time, multiple models
- generalize speculative sampling (cite)
- usually: smaller model proposes tokens, LLM validates -> lower latency
- ours: postpone evaluation of expensive model calls inside formulas
- marginal overhead over single model; up to 64\% fewer model calls
- speedup extends to prior CTG techniques expressible in model arithmetic (cite)

## Key Contributions
- Model Arithmetic framework; expresses many prior CTG approaches (Section 3)
- speculative sampling extension (Section 4)
- evaluation (Section 5): more expressive, better toxicity reduction; up to 64\% fewer calls

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In recent years Large Language Models (LLMs) have been more and more recognized for their ability to handle a wide range of tasks. In many applications, like chatbots that interact with diverse audiences such as children, students, or customers, it is crucial to precisely control and customize attributes like the vocabulary used, the linguistic style, and the emotional expression.

## Controlling Language Models

A common technique for this is prompting with natural language. Prompting is simple and makes it easy to condition the LLM to a broad attribute, but because natural language is ambiguous it is hard to express how present the attribute should be in the generated text. Prompting also can't effectively and reliably steer the model away from an attribute, because mentioning a specific topic in the prompt can by accident increase the likelihood that the model generates text about it, e.g. "do not mention cats" may make the model more likely to refer to cats. An alternative is fine-tuning the model, but this needs highly specific training data for the desired attribute, and the data also has to implicitly encode the strength of the conditioning. Controlled Text Generation (CTG) techniques try to solve this problem by steering the model during inference instead: The model is conditioned on a particular attribute a in a smoothly controllable way by biasing the token distribution of the model. Many CTG methods are inspired by Bayes rule P(\text{text}|a)\propto P(a|\text{text})P(\text{text}), and use an auxiliary model, i.e. P(a|\text{text}), to condition the LLM, i.e., P(\text{text}), towards a.

## Key Challenge: Lack of Expressive and Efficient Control for Text Generation

But these techniques have several drawbacks, including a lack of expressiveness, efficiency, and interpretability. First, to control how strong the conditioning is, a parameter \lambda is introduced in an ad-hoc way, i.e., as an exponential weight P(a|\text{text})^{\lambda}. Introducing the strength this way is possible, but it quickly becomes unintuitive because it can't be interpreted in a Bayesian way anymore, e.g., when biasing away from attributes. Also, neither prompting nor CTG methods allow multiple attributes or instructions to be combined naturally and in a controlled way with relative strength. This is because natural language in prompting is inherently ambiguous, and because CTG methods have no theoretical foundation and intuitive semantics for the biasing strength \lambda. Lastly, both CTG techniques and fine-tuning often need custom and highly specific training data for the desired attribute and can be resource-intensive since multiple models are evaluated at inference time.

## Model Arithmetic
- principled, intuitive way to combine multiple models
- orthogonal to prompting, fine-tuning, simple CTG (classifiers); incorporates them
- blend LLMs and attributes into one formula-based composite model
- Fig. 1: magical, child-like fairy tale; models M_{a} with attributes a
  - prompted \bm{{M_{\text{child}}}}: child-appropriate but not child-like
  - subtract \bm{{M_{\text{adult}}}} with weight 0.6
  - bias with classifier \bm{{C_{\text{formal}}}} to increase formality again
  - \unionop operator: magical + child-like, further bias
- not precisely expressible with prior CTG; flexible, precise control of each component
- prompting / fine-tuning for individual M and C; many prior CTG techniques as formulas (Section 3)

## Speculative Sampling
- CTG incl. model arithmetic -> more inference time, multiple models
- generalize speculative sampling (cite)
- usually: smaller model proposes tokens, LLM validates -> lower latency
- ours: postpone evaluation of expensive model calls inside formulas
- marginal overhead over single model; up to 64\% fewer model calls
- speedup extends to prior CTG techniques expressible in model arithmetic (cite)

## Key Contributions
- Model Arithmetic framework; expresses many prior CTG approaches (Section 3)
- speculative sampling extension (Section 4)
- evaluation (Section 5): more expressive, better toxicity reduction; up to 64\% fewer calls

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In recent years Large Language Models (LLMs) have been more and more recognized for their ability to handle a wide range of tasks. In many applications, like chatbots that interact with diverse audiences such as children, students, or customers, it is crucial to precisely control and customize attributes like the vocabulary used, the linguistic style, and the emotional expression.

## Controlling Language Models

A common technique for this is prompting with natural language. Prompting is simple and makes it easy to condition the LLM to a broad attribute, but because natural language is ambiguous it is hard to express how present the attribute should be in the generated text. Prompting also can't effectively and reliably steer the model away from an attribute, because mentioning a specific topic in the prompt can by accident increase the likelihood that the model generates text about it, e.g. "do not mention cats" may make the model more likely to refer to cats. An alternative is fine-tuning the model, but this needs highly specific training data for the desired attribute, and the data also has to implicitly encode the strength of the conditioning. Controlled Text Generation (CTG) techniques try to solve this problem by steering the model during inference instead: The model is conditioned on a particular attribute a in a smoothly controllable way by biasing the token distribution of the model. Many CTG methods are inspired by Bayes rule P(\text{text}|a)\propto P(a|\text{text})P(\text{text}), and use an auxiliary model, i.e. P(a|\text{text}), to condition the LLM, i.e., P(\text{text}), towards a.

## Key Challenge: Lack of Expressive and Efficient Control for Text Generation

But these techniques have several drawbacks, including a lack of expressiveness, efficiency, and interpretability. First, to control how strong the conditioning is, a parameter \lambda is introduced in an ad-hoc way, i.e., as an exponential weight P(a|\text{text})^{\lambda}. Introducing the strength this way is possible, but it quickly becomes unintuitive because it can't be interpreted in a Bayesian way anymore, e.g., when biasing away from attributes. Also, neither prompting nor CTG methods allow multiple attributes or instructions to be combined naturally and in a controlled way with relative strength. This is because natural language in prompting is inherently ambiguous, and because CTG methods have no theoretical foundation and intuitive semantics for the biasing strength \lambda. Lastly, both CTG techniques and fine-tuning often need custom and highly specific training data for the desired attribute and can be resource-intensive since multiple models are evaluated at inference time.

## Fine-Grained Control via Model Arithmetic

In this work we address these challenges and introduce model arithmetic, which is a principled and intuitive method to combine multiple models. Our method is orthogonal to prompting, fine-tuning, and simple CTG concepts like using classifiers, and it can incorporate them naturally. With model arithmetic we can blend multiple LLMs and attributes into a single composite model that is formula-based and precisely controlled. To illustrate the method, look at the simple example in Fig. 1, where we want to write a magical, child-like fairy tale. We use multiple models M_{a}, with different attributes a. On the top right there is a prompted model \bm{{M_{\text{child}}}} that already generates a story that is appropriate for children. But the text is not child-like, so we subtract a model conditioned on adults, \bm{{M_{\text{adult}}}}, with a weight of 0.6 to get a story that sounds less adult. Then to increase formality again we also bias with the classifier \bm{{C_{\text{formal}}}}. Finally we use a special \unionop operator to get a model that emphasizes both magical and child-like language, and we use it to bias the generation further and get our final result. This simple example can't be expressed precisely with prior CTG approaches and it shows how flexible model arithmetic is. That is, we can compose models in a natural way and still precisely control the impact of each component. We can also naturally incorporate paradigms like prompting or fine-tuning (for the individual M and C) and even implement many prior CTG techniques (discussed in Section 3) as simple formulas.

## Efficient Model Arithmetic via Generalized Speculative Sampling

CTG methods, including model arithmetic, can increase inference times because multiple models have to be evaluated to generate text. To counter this, we generalize speculative sampling to model arithmetic. Speculative sampling is normally used to reduce the latency of a single LLM by adding a smaller model that proposes tokens, and the LLM then validates them. We instead extend it so that we postpone the evaluation of the more expensive model calls inside model arithmetic formulas. This lets us execute model formulas made of multiple models with only marginal overhead compared to a single model, and it reduces model calls by up to 64\%. The inference speedup naturally carries over to prior CTG techniques that can be expressed in model arithmetic.

## Key Contributions

Our main contributions are:

- • Model Arithmetic: A principled framework for fine-grained CTG that allows precise control over multiple attributes. The framework can express many prior CTG approaches (Section 3).

- • An extension of speculative sampling to model arithmetic, which counters the overhead of CTG and allows efficient inference, and which naturally helps CTG techniques that are expressible in model arithmetic (Section 4).

- • An extensive qualitative and quantitative evaluation of model arithmetic (Section 5). We show that it is more expressive than prior CTG work and does better than them in toxicity reduction. We show that our extended speculative sampling reduces model calls by up to 64\%.

steps.text:
In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) [1,2,3] have been increasingly recognized for their ability to handle a wide range of tasks [4,5]. In many applications, such as chatbots interacting with diverse audiences like children, students, or customers, precise control and customization of attributes such as the vocabulary used, linguistic style, and emotional expression are crucial.

## Controlling Language Models

A common technique for this is prompting with natural language [5]. While prompting is simple and makes it easy to condition the LLM to a broad attribute, the ambiguity of natural language makes it hard to express how present that attribute should be in the generated text. Further, prompting cannot effectively steer the model away from a certain attribute in a reliable manner, as mentioning a specific topic in the prompt can inadvertently increase the likelihood of the model generating text about it [6], e.g. "do not mention cats" may increase the likelihood of the model referring to cats. One alternative is fine-tuning the model, but this requires highly specific training data for the desired attribute, which also has to implicitly encode the strength of the conditioning. Controlled Text Generation (CTG) techniques aim to solve this problem by steering the model during inference instead [7,8,9]: The model is conditioned on a particular attribute a in a smoothly controllable way, by biasing the model's token distribution. Many CTG methods are inspired by Bayes rule P(\text{text}|a)\propto P(a|\text{text})P(\text{text}), and use an auxiliary model, i.e. P(a|\text{text}), to condition the LLM, i.e., P(\text{text}), towards a.

## Key Challenge: Lack of Expressive and Efficient Control for Text Generation

These techniques, however, suffer from several drawbacks, including a lack of expressiveness, efficiency, and interpretability. First, to control the strength of the applied conditioning, a parameter \lambda is introduced in an ad-hoc manner, i.e., as an exponential weight P(a|\text{text})^{\lambda}. While possible, introducing the strength this way quickly becomes unintuitive, as it can no longer be interpreted in a Bayesian manner, e.g., when biasing away from attributes. Moreover, neither prompting nor CTG methods allow for the natural and controlled combination of multiple attributes or instructions with relative strength. This is due to the inherent ambiguity of natural language in prompting [10,11], and the absence of a theoretical foundation and intuitive semantics for the biasing strength \lambda in CTG methods. Lastly, both CTG techniques and fine-tuning often require custom and highly specific training data for the desired attribute [9,12,13,14] and can be resource-intensive [15,16] since multiple models are evaluated at inference time.

## Fine-Grained Control via Model Arithmetic

In this work, we address these challenges and introduce model arithmetic, a principled and intuitive method to combine multiple models. Our method is orthogonal to prompting, fine-tuning, and simple CTG concepts like the use of classifiers, and can naturally incorporate them. Model arithmetic enables us to blend multiple LLMs and attributes into a single, precisely controlled, formula-based composite model. To illustrate our method, consider the simple example in Fig. 1, where we aim to write a magical, child-like fairy tale. We employ multiple models M_{a}, with different attributes a. On the top right, we see a prompted model \bm{{M_{\text{child}}}} that already generates a child-appropriate story. However, the resulting text is not child-like, so we subtract an adult-conditioned model, \bm{{M_{\text{adult}}}}, with a weight of 0.6 to generate a less adult-sounding story. Then, to increase formality again, we additionally bias with classifier \bm{{C_{\text{formal}}}}. Lastly, we use a special \unionop operator to obtain a model that emphasizes both magical and child-like language and use it to further bias generation, obtaining our final result. This simple example cannot be precisely expressed with prior CTG approaches and shows the flexibility of model arithmetic: it allows us to compose models in a natural way while precisely controlling the impact of each component. Further, we can naturally incorporate paradigms such as prompting or fine-tuning (for the individual M and C) and even implement many prior CTG techniques (discussed in Section 3) as simple formulas.

## Efficient Model Arithmetic via Generalized Speculative Sampling

CTG methods, including model arithmetic, can lead to increased inference times, as multiple models need to be evaluated to generate text. To counteract this, we generalize speculative sampling [17] to model arithmetic. Speculative sampling is usually used to reduce the latency of a single LLM by augmenting it with a smaller model that proposes tokens, which the LLM then validates. In contrast, we extend it so that we postpone the evaluation of more expensive model calls within model arithmetic formulas. This allows us to execute model formulas composed of multiple models with only marginal overhead over a single model and reduces model calls by up to 64\%. The resulting inference speedup naturally extends to prior CTG techniques that can be expressed in model arithmetic [18,19,20,21].

## Key Contributions

Our core contributions include:

- • Model Arithmetic: A principled framework for fine-grained CTG, enabling precise control over multiple attributes. Our framework can express many prior CTG approaches (Section 3).

- • An extension of speculative sampling to model arithmetic, counteracting the overhead of CTG and enabling efficient inference, which naturally benefits CTG techniques expressible in model arithmetic (Section 4).

- • An extensive qualitative and quantitative evaluation of model arithmetic (Section 5). We show that it is more expressive than prior CTG work and outperforms it in toxicity reduction. We demonstrate that our extended speculative sampling reduces model calls by up to 64\%.
